deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a printed page (p. 383) from the Göttingen Royal Society of Sciences' annual report, the 'Nachrichten von der K. Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften', from late 1863. The page is a clipping filed in Riemann's 'Primzahlen' bundle as Bl. 15 (the marginal '15' is the archival foliation).

Contents:
(1) Ends the list of new foreign members: the former correspondents Hermann Kopp (Gießen) and Ludwig von Maurer (München) were elected and confirmed by the Curatorium.
(2) New correspondents of the physical class: Alexander Ecker (Freiburg) and Heinrich Credner (Hannover).
(3) New correspondents of the historical-philological class: F. F. Carlson (Stockholm), W. Giesebrecht (München), M. Haug (Puna, India), L. Lange (Gießen) and H. von Sybel (Bonn).
(4) The prize questions begin with the physical class's botanical question for November 1863, in Latin with the start of its German translation. It asks for the germination and spore function of Lycopodium, in contrast to Hofmeister's work on Selaginella, and for its true affinity among the vascular cryptogams.

The page continues onto p. 384. There the botanical question is reported as unanswered and reset for 1866. Then comes the mathematical class's prize question for November 1864: whether there are infinitely many prime pairs differing by 2, i.e. the twin prime conjecture. That twin-prime prize question, set by the Göttingen mathematical class to which Riemann belonged, is almost certainly why this printed sheet sits in Riemann's 'Primzahlen' bundle. The present page is only the lead-in to it.

There are no derivations, formulas or annotations by Riemann on this page.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed society report with no mathematical content and no handwriting by Riemann. Its only interest is that it is the lead-in to the known 1864 Göttingen twin-prime prize question, which explains its presence in the Primzahlen bundle.
transcription_corrections: The machine transcription is essentially accurate; the image confirms 'die Herrn' (not 'Herren') before Fried. Ferd. Carlson, and 'Puna (Indien)'.
The isolated '15' is a handwritten archival folio number in the right margin, not part of the printed text.
